question: What is the primary security reason for using HTTP POST instead of HTTP GET when transmitting sensitive parameter data?

options.label: A
options.text: POST requests automatically apply TLS encryption to the payload regardless of whether HTTP or HTTPS is used.
options.Explanation: Encryption depends entirely on the underlying transport protocol (HTTPS vs HTTP) rather than the choice between GET and POST methods.

options.label: B
options.text: POST parameters are included in the request body rather than the URL, preventing sensitive values from appearing in browser histories and server logs.
options.Explanation: URLs are routinely recorded in server access logs, browser histories, and bookmarks, whereas request body contents are kept out of these readable locations.

options.label: C
options.text: GET requests cannot include custom authentication tokens inside HTTP request headers.
options.Explanation: Both GET and POST requests support custom HTTP headers, such as API keys or authorization tokens.

options.label: D
options.text: POST requests establish a persistent socket connection that prevents third-party packet sniffing.
options.Explanation: POST requests follow standard HTTP connection rules and do not inherently open persistent sockets or prevent packet sniffing without HTTPS.

hints: Consider where request parameter values are displayed or recorded during routine browsing and logging.

question: How does a Webhook architecture fundamentally differ from a traditional REST API when delivering data updates?

options.label: A
options.text: Webhooks rely on client-side polling at fixed timed intervals to query server updates.
options.Explanation: Polling is a client-initiated technique common in RESTful setups, whereas Webhooks eliminate polling.

options.label: B
options.text: Webhooks proactively send data from the source server to a target listener URL as soon as an event occurs.
options.Explanation: Webhooks operate on a push model where the server sends data directly to a configured destination upon event generation.

options.label: C
options.text: Webhooks require an intermediary message queue cluster to store messages permanently before delivery.
options.Explanation: Direct Webhooks operate on a two-party basis between source and destination without requiring a message queue broker.

options.label: D
options.text: Webhooks keep a persistent two-way TCP connection open continuously for receiving streaming events.
options.Explanation: Webhooks trigger discrete HTTP POST requests per event rather than maintaining an open streaming socket.

hints: Think about which system component initiates the communication when new event data becomes available.

question: In a Publish-Subscribe (Pub/Sub) messaging system, which feature provides an advantage over direct Webhooks regarding message handling?

options.label: A
options.text: Pub/Sub brokers do not require any server infrastructure to distribute messages to consumers.
options.Explanation: Pub/Sub architectures rely on intermediate brokers (like Kafka) to manage topic routing and message delivery.

options.label: B
options.text: Pub/Sub systems persist messages to disk, allowing consumers to replay historical data streams.
options.Explanation: Storage on disk in Pub/Sub brokers ensures message durability and enables subscribers to re-read historical logs.

options.label: C
options.text: Pub/Sub architectures force data producers to manage individual HTTP POST connections for every consumer.
options.Explanation: Producers send messages only once to the central broker, which handles message fan-out to consumers automatically.

options.label: D
options.text: Pub/Sub systems restrict each published topic to a single registered consumer.
options.Explanation: A key feature of Pub/Sub is allowing multiple independent consumers to subscribe to the same topic.

hints: Focus on how event records are stored after publication and whether consumers can review past events.

question: What is a major limitation of using DOM element parsing (such as BeautifulSoup) for web data extraction?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot extract structured text elements contained within static HTML tags.
options.Explanation: DOM parsers excel at reading and organizing static text elements structured within HTML tags.

options.label: B
options.text: It requires sending a screenshot of the target webpage to a cloud server for every request.
options.Explanation: DOM parsing operates directly on the raw HTML source code without needing screenshots or visual models.

options.label: C
options.text: It is prone to breaking whenever a website modifies its visual layout or underlying HTML tags.
options.Explanation: Hardcoded CSS selectors or HTML tag paths depend heavily on exact page structures, making them brittle to web design changes.

options.label: D
options.text: It automatically executes complex client-side JavaScript code to render dynamic page updates.
options.Explanation: Basic HTML parsers only analyze the initial source code received and do not execute embedded JavaScript.

hints: Reflect on how script selectors react when a site administrator renames or rearranges layout elements.

question: Why would a data engineer use an automated browser framework like Selenium or Playwright instead of a simple HTTP client like Python's `requests`?

options.label: A
options.text: Automated browser frameworks execute JavaScript to load dynamic content and interact with user interface elements.
options.Explanation: Frameworks like Selenium control real browser engines capable of running client-side scripts and performing actions like logins.

options.label: B
options.text: Automated browser frameworks run significantly faster and consume minimal CPU memory.
options.Explanation: Running a full browser instance incurs higher overhead and memory consumption compared to lightweight HTTP requests.

options.label: C
options.text: Automated browser frameworks automatically solve all server-side CAPTCHA challenges.
options.Explanation: CAPTCHAs are designed to detect automated browser controllers, often requiring external solving mechanisms.

options.label: D
options.text: Automated browser frameworks strip out all standard HTTP headers to avoid detection.
options.Explanation: Browser automation tools send standard browser HTTP headers by default as part of operating a real browser instance.

hints: Consider how single-page web applications generate content after the initial page structure has loaded.

question: What is the primary role of a `robots.txt` file on a web server?

options.label: A
options.text: It serves as an automated firewall rule that blocks non-browser IP addresses dynamically.
options.Explanation: The file is a plain text file hosted publicly rather than an active network firewall or IP blocker.

options.label: B
options.text: It outlines a voluntary protocol informing automated crawlers which paths or pages they are permitted or forbidden to access.
options.Explanation: Web site owners use `robots.txt` to communicate crawling permissions, relying on bot operators to voluntarily respect the rules.

options.label: C
options.text: It encrypts website content to prevent unauthorized scraping of proprietary data.
options.Explanation: The `robots.txt` file provides readable directives and does not encrypt website content or prevent access cryptographically.

options.label: D
options.text: It provides mandatory API keys required for making programmatic GET requests to the domain.
options.Explanation: The file contains directives for web crawlers, not API access credentials or keys.

hints: Determine whether this file acts as a voluntary guidelines document for scrapers or a technical firewall filter.

question: Which HTTP request header should be modified in a python script to prevent an anti-scraping system from identifying the request as a basic script?

options.label: A
options.text: `Content-Type`
options.Explanation: `Content-Type` indicates the media type or data format of the request body, such as `application/json`.

options.label: B
options.text: `Authorization`
options.Explanation: `Authorization` passes security credentials like bearer tokens rather than browser identification details.

options.label: C
options.text: `User-Agent`
options.Explanation: The `User-Agent` header identifies the browser application, operating system, and software vendor making the request.

options.label: D
options.text: `Host`
options.Explanation: The `Host` header specifies the domain name of the target server and is standard across all valid requests.

hints: Select the header responsible for broadcasting client device and browser identification details to the server.

question: What is a primary drawback of utilizing vision-enabled LLMs to extract information from webpage screenshots?

options.label: A
options.text: They cannot interpret visual or non-textual layout components present on the page.
options.Explanation: Vision-enabled models excel at understanding complex visual structures, images, and non-textual page layouts.

options.label: B
options.text: They fail if the underlying HTML tag hierarchy changes slightly between page updates.
options.Explanation: Vision-enabled models operate on rendered visual pixels rather than relying on underlying HTML tag hierarchies.

options.label: C
options.text: They incur higher financial costs per request and may exhibit reliability concerns compared to traditional parsing.
options.Explanation: Processing image tokens through LLM API calls introduces higher computational expenses and potential AI hallucination risks.

options.label: D
options.text: They require writing manual Regular Expressions for every field to be extracted from the image.
options.Explanation: LLMs parse visual context naturally without requiring hardcoded regular expressions for field mapping.

hints: Consider the financial and operational trade-offs of sending images to large model APIs versus local text parsing.

question: Compared to RESTful APIs, what network efficiency advantage do Streaming APIs offer when transferring real-time data?

options.label: A
options.text: They reuse a single persistent connection, eliminating the network overhead of repeating HTTP headers for every message.
options.Explanation: Persistent connections in streaming models avoid the repeated TCP/TLS handshakes and HTTP header overhead required by REST requests.

options.label: B
options.text: They process each data item independently as a completely stateless transaction.
options.Explanation: Streaming connections are stateful and maintain an ongoing session, unlike stateless REST transactions.

options.label: C
options.text: They rely on client-initiated GET requests for every data record pushed by the server.
options.Explanation: In a streaming setup, the server pushes data proactively to the client without requiring a request per message.

options.label: D
options.text: They automatically store full historical data backups on the client side during connection drops.
options.Explanation: Streaming transport protocols deliver real-time messages but do not manage client-side historical data storage automatically.

hints: Think about what happens to connection setups and headers when sending rapid sequential data pushes.

question: Why is inserting randomized delay times between automated actions recommended when building a web crawler?

options.label: A
options.text: It prevents database transaction deadlocks when writing records to local tables.
options.Explanation: Deadlocks relate to database concurrency control mechanisms rather than request pacing on external websites.

options.label: B
options.text: It mimics human browsing behavior to reduce the likelihood of triggering rate-limiting or bot-detection systems.
options.Explanation: Varying request timing makes crawling activity appear more human, helping avoid automated rate limits and IP bans.

options.label: C
options.text: It forces the remote server to clear its application session cache between clicks.
options.Explanation: Pausing client execution does not affect or reset internal server-side caching mechanisms.

options.label: D
options.text: It grants the crawler elevated permissions to bypass website login requirements.
options.Explanation: Timing delays do not alter user authentication status or bypass access control checks.

hints: Consider how anti-bot algorithms analyze the speed and regularity of incoming user clicks.

question: An API endpoint returns an HTTP response code of `429 Too Many Requests`. How is this response classified, and what does it mean?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a 2xx Success status indicating the server processed the batch successfully.
options.Explanation: 2xx status codes indicate successful request processing rather than rate restriction errors.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a 3xx Redirection status indicating the resource has moved to a new endpoint.
options.Explanation: 3xx status codes handle URL redirects and location changes.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a 4xx Client Error status indicating that the requester has exceeded the allowed rate limits.
options.Explanation: 4xx status codes indicate client-side issues, with code 429 specifically signaling that the client sent too many requests in a given window.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a 5xx Server Error status indicating an unexpected internal database crash.
options.Explanation: 5xx status codes indicate problems originating on the server side rather than rate limits enforced on the client.

hints: Identify the meaning of the leading digit '4' in standard HTTP response status categories.

question: Which option correctly summarizes the core difference in interaction models between RESTful APIs and Webhooks?

options.label: A
options.text: RESTful APIs use a push model, whereas Webhooks use a pull model.
options.Explanation: RESTful APIs operate on a pull (request-response) model, whereas Webhooks operate on a push model.

options.label: B
options.text: RESTful APIs require the client to pull data via requests, while Webhooks push data from the server upon event triggers.
options.Explanation: Clients initiate REST requests to retrieve data on demand, whereas Webhooks deliver event data proactively to target endpoints.

options.label: C
options.text: RESTful APIs maintain open WebSocket streams, while Webhooks use offline batch file transfers.
options.Explanation: RESTful APIs use standard HTTP request-response cycles, and Webhooks send HTTP POST payloads per event.

options.label: D
options.text: RESTful APIs can only return binary image files, while Webhooks exclusively deliver relational tables.
options.Explanation: Both API methods can handle structured formats like JSON or XML.

hints: Identify who initiates the transaction when data needs to move from source to destination.
